nameStory: Common stonewort gets its name from its rough, crusty texture that feels almost like stone when you run it between your fingers. The 'wort' part is an old English word meaning plant, so this is literally the 'stone plant.' Despite feeling mineral-like, it's actually a fascinating green alga that coats itself with calcium carbonate from the water!
description: Common stonewort is a submerged green alga that looks more like an underwater plant than what most people picture when they hear 'algae.' It grows in branching, feathery clusters with thin, segmented stems that radiate out like the spokes of a wheel. The whole plant has a distinctive rough, gritty texture from calcium deposits and can form dense underwater meadows in clear ponds and lakes. It typically grows 6-12 inches tall but can reach up to 2 feet in ideal conditions.

idTips.label: Crusty texture
idTips.description: Run the plant between your fingers - it feels rough and gritty, almost like sandpaper, due to calcium carbonate deposits coating the surface

idTips.label: Whorled branches
idTips.description: Thin, needle-like branches radiate out from joints on the main stem like spokes on a wheel, typically in groups of 6-12

idTips.label: Segmented stems
idTips.description: The main stem is divided into distinct sections or nodes, like bamboo, with branches emerging only at these joint points

idTips.label: Spiky bark cells
idTips.description: Look closely at the stem surface with a hand lens - you'll see tiny spikes protruding between the elongated cells that make up the 'bark'

idTips.label: Musky odor
idTips.description: When crushed or disturbed, it releases a distinctive skunky, sulfurous smell that's quite unmistakable

habitat: Common stonewort thrives in clear, calcium-rich ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. You'll find it in shallow to moderately deep water (2-15 feet) where sunlight can still penetrate to the bottom. It prefers hard water environments and often indicates good water quality since it's sensitive to pollution.

seasonality.spring: Plants begin active growth as water warms, appearing as small tufts of green growth on lake and pond bottoms. New shoots emerge from overwintering structures.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full, bushy underwater meadows visible in clear water. This is the best time for identification when all features are most pronounced.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline but are still identifiable. Reproductive structures may be visible as small orange or reddish bumps on the branches.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground growth dies back, leaving behind specialized overwintering buds that will sprout next spring. Very difficult to find and identify.

funFact: Common stonewort is actually more closely related to land plants than to other algae - it's like finding a 400-million-year-old missing link living in your local pond! Scientists consider stoneworts to be among the closest living relatives to the very first plants that crawled out of ancient seas to colonize land.
confusionNotes: It's most often confused with submerged flowering plants like water milfoil or hornwort, but the telltale gritty, crusty texture immediately sets stonewort apart - no true aquatic plant feels like sandpaper! Remember: if it's rough and crusty underwater, it's probably a stonewort.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'stonewort,' this species is actually a green alga, not a true plant with flowers and seeds. The name can be confusing since many '-wort' plants are flowering plants, but stoneworts represent an ancient lineage that predates true plants by millions of years.
compareHints: Common stonewort can be distinguished from fragile stonewort by its distinctive spikes between the bark cells - fragile stonewort lacks these tiny projections and feels slightly less rough. Compared to delicate stonewort, common stonewort is more robust and has a coarser texture. The spiky bark cell feature is the most reliable way to separate common stonewort from its close relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Fragile stonewort is distinguished from its relatives like common stonewort and Braun's stonewort primarily through microscopic features of its reproductive structures, which have distinctive surface patterns.
Compared to its relatives, delicate stonewort is the most fragile of the New England stoneworts - much more so than the sturdier common stonewort or even fragile stonewort.
Chara zeylanica is extremely rare in New England with only 2 recorded observations, making it much less common than fragile stonewort or common stonewort.

Braun's stonewort differs from its relatives like common stonewort and fragile stonewort by lacking cortication - the bark-like ridged coating that makes other species feel textured along their main stems.
